questions.problem:
Given that $J(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x,$ calculate ${J}^{′}(t)$ for $t\in R$ by differentiating under the integral sign.

${J}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\,$
{{field-1}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as differentiating under the integral sign.

We wish to compute ${J}^{′}(t),$ where

$$
J(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
{J}^{′}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}]\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}] & =2(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\  & =2(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t){\int }_{0}^{1}(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{1}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}^{′}(t) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(\frac{3}{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(3-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

I. ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$

II. ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{t}{1+{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$

III. ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(x+t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=|x-t|.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ However, the partial derivative

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\{\begin{aligned}-1,\,x>t \\ 1,\,x<t\end{aligned}
$$

does *not* exist whenever $x=t={t}_{0},$ and is therefore not defined everywhere on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{t}{1+{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{(1+{x}^{2}+{t}^{2})-2{t}^{2}}{(1+{x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}}=\frac{1+{x}^{2}-{t}^{2}}{(1+{x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{(x+t+1)^{3}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\frac{3}{(x+t+1)^{4}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (0,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

I. ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$

II. ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=|x-t|.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ However, the partial derivative

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\{\begin{aligned}-1,\,x>t \\ 1,\,x<t\end{aligned}
$$

does *not* exist whenever $x=t={t}_{0},$ and is therefore not defined everywhere on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)={e}^{t{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}={x}^{2}{e}^{t{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{x}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}<0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-\infty ,0)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(x-t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{I}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}(2{t}^{5})=20{t}^{9}.

questions.problem:
Given that $K(t)={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{3}\,\text{d}x,$ calculate ${K}^{′}(t)$ for $t\in R$ by differentiating under the integral sign.

${K}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(\,$
{{field-1}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as differentiating under the integral sign.

We wish to compute ${K}^{′}(t),$ where

$$
K(t)={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
{K}^{′}(t)={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{3}]\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{3}] & =3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\  & =3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) \\  & =-3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}-3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t){\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral. We first expand the squared term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t){|}_{-1}^{1}+x{cos}^{2}⁡(t){|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3}))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))+({cos}^{2}⁡(t)-(-{cos}^{2}⁡(t))) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+2{cos}^{2}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{′}(t) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot (\frac{2}{3}+2{cos}^{2}⁡(t)) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)(1+3{cos}^{2}⁡(t)).\end{aligned}
$$
